<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Automatic evaluation of faithfulness increasingly relies on a large language model acting as a judge, yet the most reliable judges are proprietary frontier models.
Their per-call cost, rate limits, and off-premises inference, however, make them ill-suited to the continuous, high-throughput monitoring that benchmarking and production use demand.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">In this work we investigate three fundamental questions: whether a panel of cheap open-weight judges (<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B parameters) can be aggregated to stand in for a frontier one, what the substitution sacrifices in agreement (Cohen’s <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>) and accuracy, and when it is worth making.
To address them, we propose RAIM, an aggregation scheme robust to the members’ correlated errors, which couples:
(<math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>) a cross-fitted stacked logistic regression that fits the members’ weights jointly, therefore penalising weaker judges echoing a stronger one;
and (<math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>) an admissibility test that, read from the members’ own outputs, identifies a regime in which aggregating them improves on their best member and stays within reach of the frontier judge.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">We instantiate RAIM under ten judges drawn from disjoint families and we measure the substitution across eight faithfulness benchmarks.
Read as paired differences against <span id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Claude Sonnet</span>, the substitution clearly improves on one benchmark and clearly worsens on three (only two by a non-negligible margin), leaving the remaining four unresolved.
The panel retains a median <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="93\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>93</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">93\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the frontier judge’s <math id="abstract1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> agreement and gives up only <math id="abstract1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9</annotation></semantics></math> points of balanced accuracy on average.
Inference runs at a sixty-fourth of the frontier’s price at conventional cloud rates, or at the electricity cost on premises, so the operative expense is a one-time in-domain calibration of some fifty to a hundred labelled records, amortised over a few tens of thousands of evaluated items.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.4" class="ltx_p">Against the literature, the panel is competitive with purpose-trained detectors on their home benchmarks, losing <math id="abstract1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.3</annotation></semantics></math> points of accuracy to <span id="abstract1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GPT-4o</span>  and <math id="abstract1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.9</annotation></semantics></math> to the best <span id="abstract1.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span> leaderboard model;
yet the strongest detector we reran falls <math id="abstract1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6</annotation></semantics></math> points behind on our grounded sets, and cannot score the ungrounded ones.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.5" class="ltx_p">In conclusion, whether pursuing the aggregation is worthwhile depends on the members themselves, making the gain auditable from how widely competence is spread across them and how far their errors decorrelate — both read at no further cost off the aggregator’s calibration set.
If several capable members err on different items, the panel improves on its best judge and approaches the frontier;
conversely, where one dominates, the stacker recovers the leader, yet only there does the frontier remain materially ahead.
A panel of cheap judges can therefore stand in for a frontier one at a small fraction of the cost wherever this audit admits it.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords:</span>
LLM-as-a-judge · hallucination detection · faithfulness evaluation · judge ensembles · error correlation · open-weight models · cost-efficient evaluation.</p>
  
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Automatic evaluation of faithfulness –whether a given claim, a retrieved passage, or a model’s output is supported by its source or constitutes a hallucination– increasingly relies on a large language model acting as a judge (LLM-as-a-judge; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">84</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>).
Single-model judges, however, carry systematic biases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> and are reported to reach human-level agreement only at scales well above the small models (<math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{&lt;}10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{&lt;}10</annotation></semantics></math>B parameters) a deployer can serve locally <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.
As a consequence, the judges one can most rely on are large proprietary models served from the cloud, so each evaluated item is a metered, rate-limited call, whose cost is small individually yet adds up at scale, and which sends the text off-premises to an endpoint the deployer does not control.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Three main strategies have been proposed to reduce this dependence: <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">escalate</em>, keeping a frontier judge but calling it only where a cheap model is unsure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>; <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">specialise</em>, training one small model expressly for the task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>; or <em id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">aggregate</em>, running several cheap judges and combining their verdicts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>.
Escalation, however, retains a frontier judge as a fallback, and we read it as a complementary solution (Appendix <a href="#A12" title="Appendix L Extended related work ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">L</span></a>).
Specialists are typically trained for reference-conditioned verification and, whilst holding an advantage on home ground, they cannot score a task that supplies no reference at all.
Moreover, they are reported to generalise poorly off the distribution they were trained on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, as we confirm by running them ourselves across our suite (Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Purpose-trained cheap judges off their home benchmark ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>).
Specialisation and aggregation both remove the frontier model from the loop, as the constraints beyond price actually require (i.e. on-premises inference, no rate limit, no deprecation).
Of the two, we pursue aggregation, the only one that needs no training of model weights and keeps the generality just noted.
The practical question is therefore not whether a frontier judge is good, but whether one has to be paid for: can several cheap, open-weight judges, run locally and combined, stand in for it?
We refer to Appendix <a href="#A12" title="Appendix L Extended related work ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">L</span></a> for a deeper account of these routes, of the noisy-voter literature the aggregator inherits, and of how recent panel studies compare with ours (Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Roadmap to the appendices ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> maps every appendix to the claim it supports).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The intuition that the <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">aggregate</em> solution might work is the classical one behind ensembling and the Condorcet jury theorem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, and a panel of small judges has indeed been reported to track human ratings better than a single frontier model at a fraction of its price <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>.
That intuition rests, however, on an assumption which is fragile for exactly these estimators.
Weak voters rival a strong one when their errors are <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">independent</em>, whereas judges drawn from a common pretraining prior err together <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>, <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.
Indeed, a panel of nine frontier judges is reported to carry only about two effective independent votes, leaving the best single judge unbeaten <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
What this line of work leaves open is hence not if a cheap panel pays on average, but under which conditions it pays at all, and what the substitution costs where it does not.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We take up both questions together, and we do so by introducing RAIM (Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models; Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), an aggregation scheme that couples two components.
It aggregates a panel of cheap open-weight judges by (<math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>) a cross-fitted stacked meta-learner, which fits member weights <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">jointly</em> and so discounts a judge echoing a stronger one, instead of weighting each by its own accuracy;
and it pairs that with (<math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>) an admissibility test, read off the single members, which identifies the regime in which aggregating them pays.
Together, the two make the aggregation <em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">robust</em>, where a plain ensemble is only redundant.
We instantiate the scheme with ten small judges from disjoint families, and study its behaviour across eight faithfulness benchmarks and against a ladder of comparators ordered by the labelled information each of them consumes.
Combining noisy voters is itself classical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite>, and we adopt the simplest form that expresses the joint weighting correlated errors require.
A heavier estimator would consume labels the calibration budget cannot afford, and would offer a rival explanation for whatever the panel gains; with ten fitted coefficients, instead, the gain becomes attributable to the members alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The result proves conditional.
A frontier judge is not, in general, replaced without cost, yet that cost is small and concentrated;
against its own best member, conversely, the panel improves on all four core grounded sets, though the sample resolves that improvement on only one of them, with no clear worsening anywhere.
The eight benchmarks therefore yield an account of <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">which</em> tasks fall on which side, with the members’ joint distribution of <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">competence</em> and the <em id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">correlation</em> of their errors at the centre: aggregation pays where several judges are individually capable and disagree in their mistakes, and falls back on the leader where one judge dominates or all of them are weak and err together.</p>
</div>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The RAIM protocol at a glance.
Ten cheap open-weight judges (<math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B) each score a candidate against its source, and a cross-fitted stacked logistic regression combines their votes into one verdict.
The same calibration set yields an admissibility test, read off the members, which identifies a regime in which aggregating them pays.
The verdict is read against the CV-best single judge <em id="S1.F1.6.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">of</em> the panel, and against a paid frontier judge the panel is meant to replace.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contributions.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We summarise our contributions as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(i)</span> We introduce RAIM, an aggregation scheme coupling (<math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>) a cross-fitted meta-learner that fits the members’ weights jointly with (<math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>) a label-cheap admissibility test which, read off the members’ own verdicts rather than the panel’s, identifies a regime in which aggregating them pays.
Along with it, we adopt a comparator ladder of baselines and a decision rule built on paired differences, which keeps the direction of an effect apart from the power to resolve it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(ii)</span> We instantiate RAIM on ten judges of <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B parameters from disjoint families over eight faithfulness benchmarks, releasing the whole chain from generation to analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(iii)</span> We measure what the panel trades off against a frontier judge, finding that it retains a median <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="93\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>93</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">93\%</annotation></semantics></math> of <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Claude Sonnet</span>’s <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> and falls materially behind on two of the eight benchmarks.
Against the purpose-trained detectors that are its sharpest competitors, it stays competitive on the benchmarks those detectors were trained for, and leads them elsewhere.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(iv)</span> We price the substitution, including the labels the aggregator consumes, showing that inference runs at a sixty-fourth of the frontier’s cost at rented cloud rates, so the operative expense is the one-time in-domain calibration and not the evaluation:
fifty labelled records suffice for the aggregator to beat a free majority vote on seven of eight sets, and a hundred are enough to approach full supervision, which places the break-even against the frontier judge between <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>40,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="81{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>81,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">81{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> evaluated items.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(v)</span> We identify what decides the outcome, and it is not the grounded-versus-ungrounded contrast one would expect but a property of the members: how widely competence is spread across them, and how far their errors decorrelate.
We confirm this finding at the item level, over the <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}998" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,998</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}998</annotation></semantics></math> items on which the panel’s own leader errs, and we show both coordinates to be readable from the calibration set the aggregator already consumes, so the regime is known by the time the panel is fitted.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>The RAIM protocol</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let us consider a panel made of <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> members (LLMs) which, given a prompt, return one binary verdict on a candidate statement: <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">supported</em> (gold<math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0</annotation></semantics></math>) or <em id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hallucinated</em>/unsupported (gold<math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=1</annotation></semantics></math>).
We evaluate the panel on two tasks: <em id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">grounded</em> faithfulness, where the candidate is judged against an explicit reference; and <em id="S2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ungrounded</em> factuality, where it is judged against world knowledge alone.
Datasets are built class-balanced, and items are grouped into clusters by the source record or grounding document they derive from (Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Dataset construction ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>).
In what follows, we describe the RAIM protocol in two steps: the framework first and the instantiation after.
We defer the description of the admissibility test to §<a href="#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" title="The admissibility test. ‣ 3.3. The competence/correlation account ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, where the quantities it reads are defined.
The judge prompt, the decoding settings, and the coverage audit are deferred to Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Judge roster, prompt, and coverage ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a>, and the per-dataset item construction to Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Dataset construction ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Aggregation and the comparator ladder.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> votes per query, we adopt a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">stacked logistic regression</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite> to aggregate them: a vote over the votes, taking the member verdicts as its features and the gold label as its target, so that each member earns a weight from how well its verdict predicts the truth w.r.t. the others.
Writing <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> for member <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s verdict on an item (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\{1,\dots,N_{v}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>v</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\{1,\dots,N_{v}\}</annotation></semantics></math>; abstentions imputed as <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, tested in Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Judge roster, prompt, and coverage ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a>), the meta-learner estimates</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">fitting <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> by penalised maximum likelihood under an untuned <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Of weight <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/C</annotation></semantics></math> on the squared coefficients, left at the conventional <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=1</annotation></semantics></math>; with only ten features the fit is insensitive to the choice, and the smallest sets (<span id="footnote1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CNN</span>, <span id="footnote1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WiCE</span>, <span id="footnote1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FActScore</span>) are where it matters most.</span></span></span>.
The coefficients <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are what a vote weighted by each member’s own accuracy cannot express: they are fitted <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">jointly</em>, so a member that merely echoes a stronger one is discounted rather than counted twice, and a member that is informative but anti-correlated with gold can take a negative weight.
To avoid leakage, the stacker is fitted by 5-fold cross-fitting, so that every item’s stacked prediction is produced out-of-fold.
A verdict is read at the conventional <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> threshold, which also breaks the unweighted majority’s ties at <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{v}=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{v}=10</annotation></semantics></math>.
Fitting <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, however, requires gold labels, a cost we measure in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> and price in §<a href="#S4" title="4. Standing in for a frontier judge ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the stacked panel against a ladder of comparators, ordered by the labelled information each of them consumes.
The unweighted majority panel, the average member, and the unsupervised Dawid–Skene aggregator
need no labels and are fully deployable; the best-on-average single is one global label-based selection deployed everywhere; the cross-validated (CV) best single, selected on a development split, and the stacked panel are both supervised and both evaluated strictly out-of-fold; the oracle best single, selecting the argmax on the very test set it is scored against, is the most generous yet undeployable comparator; and above them all sits the one the panel is meant to replace rather than beat, a proprietary frontier judge, named and read in §<a href="#S4" title="4. Standing in for a frontier judge ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics and the decision rule.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our primary metric is Cohen’s <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, which rescales the observed agreement <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> with the gold label by the agreement <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> that a random sample would produce, so that only agreement above chance is credited: <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=(p_{o}-p_{e})/(1-p_{e})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=(p_{o}-p_{e})/(1-p_{e})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We accompany it with balanced accuracy (<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">bacc</span>), i.e. the mean of the two per-class recalls (on our class-balanced sets coinciding with plain accuracy), which accounts for an abstention from the opposite side: an abstained item is dropped from <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>, yet charged in <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">bacc</span> as an error against its own class; Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Judge roster, prompt, and coverage ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a> audits the denominator asymmetry this creates between an abstaining baseline and the always-imputing panel.
All quantities carry <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> paired cluster-bootstrap percentile intervals over <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=2000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=2000</annotation></semantics></math> resamples of the clustering unit, so that co-clustered instances always resample together, and every central estimate is followed by its <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\text{lower},\text{upper}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext>lower</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>upper</mtext><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\text{lower},\text{upper}]</annotation></semantics></math> interval.
When comparing two methods, every verdict is read from the paired difference of their scores: within each draw, both sides are recomputed on the same resampled clusters, so that scores are always compared on the very same items; this is materially sharper than assessing if the marginal intervals overlap, since the two scores rise and fall together across draws<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            On <span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span> the stacked panel spans <math id="footnote2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.695,0.756]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.695</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.756</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.695,0.756]</annotation></semantics></math> and its best single judge <math id="footnote2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.658,0.727]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.658</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.727</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.658,0.727]</annotation></semantics></math>, largely overlapping, while their paired difference is <math id="footnote2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.032" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.032</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.032</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="footnote2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[+0.004,+0.060]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.004</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.060</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[+0.004,+0.060]</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On that basis we define three verdicts: a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">win</em> requires the stacked <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> to significantly beat the CV-best single, i.e. the lower bound of the paired difference to exceed zero; a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">clean win</em> additionally requires it to beat the oracle single; a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">tie</em> is a difference straddling zero, and admits no intermediate grade, though where a tie’s interval comes close to excluding zero we report its one-sided <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>.
Every paired difference we report –that one included, and equally those against the average member, the label-free aggregators, or the frontier judge of §<a href="#S4" title="4. Standing in for a frontier judge ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>– is described in one four-way form: an <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">improvement</em> or a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">worsening</em>, <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">clear</em> where the <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> paired interval, uncorrected for multiplicity, excludes zero and <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unresolved</em> where it does not (Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Judge roster, prompt, and coverage ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a> gives Holm-adjusted <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values for the best-single contrasts).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks and judges.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run RAIM on eight faithfulness benchmarks<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Question-answering grounded: <span id="footnote3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span> and <span id="footnote3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span>; claim-verification grounded: <span id="footnote3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WiCE</span>, <span id="footnote3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSum</span>, <span id="footnote3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CNN</span>, and <span id="footnote3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ExpertQA</span> (from <span id="footnote3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span>); ungrounded: <span id="footnote3.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FActScore</span> and <span id="footnote3.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TruthfulQA</span>.
</span></span></span>: six <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">grounded</em> and two <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ungrounded</em> (Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Full per-dataset tables ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>, Table <a href="#A9.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix I Full per-dataset tables ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>).
Two of the six grounded sets are held back from the primary tally on measurability grounds: <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CNN</span> is too small to power the paired contrast (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=114" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>114</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=114</annotation></semantics></math>), and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ExpertQA</span> is a low-headroom task, with no published method on the <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span> leaderboard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite> exceeding a <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">bacc</span> of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\approx}\,61\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn> 61</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\approx}\,61\%</annotation></semantics></math> (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>, Table <a href="#A6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Harness calibration. ‣ Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).
The primary denominator is therefore the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">core grounded</em> four –<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSum</span>, and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WiCE</span>– with all six grounded sets as a secondary denominator and the suite of eight as the widest.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Over those benchmarks, we set <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{v}=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{v}=10</annotation></semantics></math>, instantiating the panel with ten open-weight instruction-tuned judges of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B parameters drawn from disjoint model families to diversify failure modes: <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Llama</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mistral</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Gemma</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Phi</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Yi</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Command-R</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GLM</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Granite</span>, and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Falcon</span> being the family tag by which we refer to each throughout (for details see Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Judge roster, prompt, and coverage ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a>, Table <a href="#A11.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ The roster. ‣ Appendix K Judge roster, prompt, and coverage ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>).
A member returning no parseable verdict is recorded as abstaining.
The prompt supplies the task definition, and takes one of two frames: the rubric we label <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">def_on</span> on the four question-answering sets, scaffolding the tuple (question, evidence, candidate) on <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span> and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span> and dropping the evidence block on the ungrounded <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FActScore</span> and <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TruthfulQA</span>; and a MiniCheck-style <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite> <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.16" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">claim-support</em> frame, pairing (document, claim), on the four <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span> claim-verification sets (<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.18" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WiCE</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSum</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CNN</span>, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ExpertQA</span>), whose structure requires it (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>).
The frame is fixed per dataset and identical across all ten members and the frontier judge.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Core results</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the study’s core results in three steps: first the panel measured against the other ways of combining the same ten votes, then against the best single judge <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inside</em> it, and finally the member-level account of when either contrast comes out in the panel’s favour (§<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. The competence/correlation account ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>); the comparison with the frontier judge is deferred to §<a href="#S4" title="4. Standing in for a frontier judge ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> carries all of it on one comparator ladder, whose columns are ordered by the labelled information each baseline consumes: from the label-free aggregators a deployer can always run, through the one globally best member, to the per-dataset best single and the frontier judge.
Reading a row left to right is therefore reading what each increment of supervision buys.
The full per-method ladders and the rescue and aggregator contrasts are in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Full per-dataset tables ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> (Table <a href="#A9.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix I Full per-dataset tables ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>).</p>
</div>
