</section>
<section id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multiplicity.</h4>

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The suite runs the same paired test over the eight datasets, so the question of what the eight verdicts mean together deserves an explicit answer.
We report every interval per comparison and we read the eight as a description of where the panel stands rather than as a family of confirmatory tests.
Each dataset asks its own question, and the paper’s claim is the characterisation of the regimes, not a single pooled effect.
The Holm check <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> nonetheless matters, because one verdict –the <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span> win– is load-bearing, and a reader is entitled to ask whether it survives being treated as one test among several.
Over the four core grounded sets, the primary denominator declared in §<a href="#S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" title="Benchmarks and judges. ‣ 2. The RAIM protocol ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, it does: <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span>’s raw one-sided <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.012" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.012</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.012</annotation></semantics></math> adjusts to <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.048" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.048</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.048</annotation></semantics></math>.
The other three do not, and the correction bites hardest where the body already reports an unresolved difference: <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">XSum</span>, the closest to resolution per comparison (one-sided <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.045" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.045</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.045</annotation></semantics></math>), adjusts to <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.135" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.135</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.135</annotation></semantics></math>; <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WiCE</span> to <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.155" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.155</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.155</annotation></semantics></math>; <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span> to <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.280" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.280</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.280</annotation></semantics></math>.
As a consequence, the adjustment changes no verdict in the paper, since an unresolved improvement is reported as a tie in the first place.
We read this as a boundary and not a reassurance.
Over the widest denominator, with all eight datasets treated as one family, <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span>’s win would adjust to <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.096</annotation></semantics></math> and would not survive at the conventional level.
The win is therefore a claim about the core grounded four.
What the suite is evidence for is the ordering of the eight datasets, on which §<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. The competence/correlation account ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> rests and which no single <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-value can carry.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The missing-vote denominator confound.</h4>

<div id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A method’s <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> is scored over its own non-abstaining set: because the stacker imputes every missing member vote it is always scored on the full item set, whereas a single-judge baseline is scored only on the items where it returned a parseable verdict; whenever that baseline under-covers, the delta (<span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">stacked <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math> best-single</span>) therefore compares two different denominators.
We surface each baseline’s committed-<math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> –i.e. the number of items it actually returned a verdict on, out of the dataset’s <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>– beside every estimate (Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math>), and use the companion balanced accuracy, which charges abstention on the full denominator, as a check;
where the two metrics agree, the verdict does not depend on how abstentions are handled.
The one headline contrast with a materially under-covering baseline is <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span>, where the CV-best judge (<span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Granite</span>) abstains on roughly <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17\%</annotation></semantics></math> of items (<math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}653" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,653</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}653</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> scored).
Restricting the comparison to that common denominator leaves the gap essentially unchanged: <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.031" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.031</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.031</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[+0.003,+0.058]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.003</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.058</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[+0.003,+0.058]</annotation></semantics></math> against the full-denominator <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.032" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.032</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.032</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[+0.004,+0.060]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.004</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.060</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[+0.004,+0.060]</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>’s prevalence correction absorbing the dropped items.
The residual asymmetry, moreover, runs against the panel.
The items <span id="A11.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Granite</span> abstains on are harder and disproportionately hallucinated, so scoring the baseline only where it was willing to answer flatters it, and the reported gap understates the panel’s advantage.
The verdict is therefore conservative rather than inflated.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A12" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix L </span>Extended related work</h2>

<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM-as-judge and its limitations.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using a strong language model to score the outputs of another has become the default substitute for human annotation where gold labels are scarce or ill-defined <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">84</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>.
Single-model judges, however, carry systematic biases –positional and verbosity effects, and a self-preference for their own generations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>– and are reported to reach human-level agreement only well above the <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B scale, no judge in that class clearing the bar <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, which motivates cheaper judges and combinations of them.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Panels of judges.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The closest line of work likewise replaces the single judge with a panel.
However, it typically does so whilst asking whether the substitution pays on average, rather than under what conditions it pays.
In particular, the Panel of LLM Evaluators (PoLL) reports that an ensemble of smaller judges from disjoint families can correlate with humans better than a single frontier judge, at a fraction of the cost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>.
Related frameworks extend the idea with richer aggregation and to more subjective tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">83</a>]</cite>, whereas cascaded selective evaluation escalates to an expensive judge only where the cheap ones are unsure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.
The self-consistency family, by contrast, asks an orthogonal question: it resamples one model rather than combining judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, and so catches arbitrary errors rather than the systematic ones a panel shares.
Along this line, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ricco et al. [65]</a></cite> find the self-consistency signal to be geometric for small models, with genuine answers to a prompt clustering more tightly in sentence-embedding space than hallucinated ones;
the authors propagate labels from some thirty to fifty responses per model, where responses are judged by a frontier model — the kind of judging a cheap panel could take over.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Noisy-voter aggregation.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Combining imperfect voters is a classical problem well beyond LLMs.
Latent-variable models estimate each annotator’s reliability without gold labels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, their descendants adding item difficulty <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>, annotator spamming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, or a Bayesian prior over each annotator’s confusion matrix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, to cite a few.
Similarly, weak-supervision frameworks estimate the accuracies and correlations of many noisy sources <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>.
Finally, in ensemble learning, the <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diversity</em> of the members’ errors is the standard explanation of what combining them gains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, although diversity measures predict that gain only weakly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>.
In their unsupervised use, however, all these models infer a member’s reliability from its agreement with a latent consensus.
On a correlated panel that consensus <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">is</em> the shared error, so the obstruction Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> documents for Dawid–Skene applies to them by construction, as it does to label-free aggregators designed for LLM judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Extensions that account for the dependence between members do relieve the obstruction, but only under assumptions of their own, which Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> spells out <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
We therefore run Dawid–Skene as the representative of the family, and leave open whether a dependence-aware extension recovers member competence on panels as correlated as ours.
Furthermore, the aggregators designed for LLM judges do not escape the best single member either: on <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TruthfulQA</span>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. [70]</a></cite> report every aggregator they compare (over <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>B judges), their own included, below the strongest member (<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="68.77" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>68.77</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">68.77</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="69.84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>69.84</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">69.84</annotation></semantics></math>).
They also select their checkpoints on <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="250" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>250</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250</annotation></semantics></math> labelled items, well above the fifty records with which our stacker already clears the vote on seven of eight sets (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Correlated errors.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work consistently reports that language models, judges among them, violate the independence assumption underlying naive ensembling.
In particular, CARE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>]</cite> traces the violation to latent confounders that the judges share and that correlate their errors.
Beyond judges, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [36]</a></cite> measure the phenomenon across more than <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="350" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>350</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">350</annotation></semantics></math> models: errors overlap heavily and, decisively for a panel, correlation <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rises</em> with model accuracy, even across providers and architectures.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goel et al. [20]</a></cite> observe the same trend under a chance-adjusted error-similarity metric across <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="130" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>130</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">130</annotation></semantics></math> leaderboard models.
This is what makes a panel of <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cheap</em> judges a more interesting instrument than a panel of strong ones, and not simply a thriftier one.
Indeed, the decorrelation on which aggregation feeds is most available where individual competence is lowest, which is also why our roster is drawn from disjoint families at the <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B scale.
However, since open-ended generations are markedly homogeneous across them, disjoint families offer no guarantee of diversity <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">a priori</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.
For this reason, the admissibility test reads the correlation coordinate off the calibration set instead of presuming it from the roster.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Recent panels and ensembles of LLM judges.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several recent and concurrent studies address questions close to ours.
In what follows, we set each against our account, noting where it agrees and where it departs in task, judges, or aggregator.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kohli [40]</a></cite> reports that a panel of nine <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">frontier</em> judges carries only about two effective independent votes on <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">nli</span> tasks, falling <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="22" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>22</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">22</annotation></semantics></math> points below what independent voting would give, and leaving the best single judge unbeaten.
We do not read this as a contrary finding.
Indeed, their nine judges are worth about two independent votes, and on the four of our sets whose members are worth fewer (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS0.SSS0.Px6" title="Effective independence against a frontier panel. ‣ Appendix B The competence/correlation account in full ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>) we too find that aggregation recovers the leader and no more.
This is also how our account reconciles that result with the optimistic panel literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu and Rao [86]</a></cite> likewise treat a labelling budget as the binding constraint, but for a different decision: which aggregator family, and how many judges, the available labels can support once a panel is to be run.
On preference and summarisation benchmarks, with six <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math>B open judges and one <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">api</span> model, they report scalar or reliability aggregation beating a joint-table calibrator in <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> dataset–budget cells, current judge outputs being often “additive or redundant”.
This supports the redundancy premise we build on, and is why we do not pursue a richer aggregator.
In the same vein, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li [49]</a></cite> reports, on pairwise reward benchmarks, that a calibrated full panel beats discarding judges by accuracy, which is what our fitted coefficients show when the weakest of the ten members still draws a large weight (Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Full per-dataset tables ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Closer to our setting, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laddha et al. [44]</a></cite> evaluate sixteen small judges (<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.6</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14</annotation></semantics></math>B) for the same reasons as ours (cost, privacy, and silently changing model versions), and report that the best of ten three-judge juries drawn from their top five judges gains only <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.06" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.06</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.06</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy points over the best individual judge.
Their leading judges share most of their mistakes, which would place those juries on the correlated side of our plane (Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3. The competence/correlation account ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a)), where the admissibility test rejects a panel.
They leave decorrelated panels aside as needing “per-instance error knowledge unavailable at deployment time”, whereas the test reads both coordinates off fifty to a hundred labelled records (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>).
Moreover, they do not price the substitution against a proprietary judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From a more analytical angle, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ali [2]</a></cite> proposes a law for a weighted vote of two models, in which the lift over the stronger one grows with the weaker one’s accuracy and with their accuracy-adjusted complementarity, and shrinks with their accuracy gap.
It is a pairwise analogue of our account, in which the gap plays the part of our dominant leader.
Its claim that raw correctness correlation alone predicts almost nothing (<math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}\leq 0.09" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.09</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}\leq 0.09</annotation></semantics></math>) is indeed consistent with our correlation coordinate being the weaker of the two when read alone (Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B The competence/correlation account in full ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>).
In a similar spirit, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim [35]</a></cite> reports that five common diversity measures largely re-express capability as predictors of majority-vote gain, leaving only a modest residual in which more shared error means less gain;
this entanglement is why we report competence and error-correlation as separate coordinates.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou and Lin [85]</a></cite> propose the nearest analogue of our admissibility test.
They flag a three-judge factuality panel as unsafe when a labelled calibration probe shows correlated false negatives, at thresholds fixed in advance, and route the panel’s accepts to grounded verification.
Their flag, however, reads a correlation coordinate alone, and escalates to a reference rather than to a frontier judge.
Outside faithfulness, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grayzel [22]</a></cite> reports three larger open-weight judges to be statistically indistinguishable from two frontier judges on pass/fail proof grading, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost.
That substitution is priced per call, however, with no calibration outlay and no account of when it holds.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, and concurrently with this work, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hossain et al. [27]</a></cite> report the design-effect <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{eff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>eff</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{eff}}</annotation></semantics></math> of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kohli [40]</a></cite> for a panel of ten judges on preference data.
Those ten judges, however, are only five open models under <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>B, four of them checkpoints of our roster, each run under two prompts.
Among these, they report an average error correlation of <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.21" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.21</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.21</annotation></semantics></math>, worth about <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.5</annotation></semantics></math> independent judges, and a stronger dependence still among three frontier judges.
Their two dependence-aware filters then rank items for retention rather than weight members, and neither is reported to improve on the plain majority on eight <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span> components.
Conversely, we pair the correlation coordinate with a competence one, fit the weights on labels, and price the substitution of a frontier judge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Where this work sits.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Read together, these works measure how dependent a panel’s errors are, choose an aggregator once a panel is to be run, or flag when a cheap panel should escalate.
Our questions sit one step earlier: whether to run a cheap local panel <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">at all</em> in place of a paid frontier judge, at what price once its calibration labels are counted, and how a deployer is to tell in advance.
As to adoption, the panel falls materially behind the frontier judge on only two of our eight benchmarks, both in the dominant-leader regime (§<a href="#S4" title="4. Standing in for a frontier judge ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
As for the price, the panel holds a median <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="93\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>93</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">93\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the frontier judge’s <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> at a sixty-fourth of its inference cost, and its one-time calibration breaks even between some <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>40,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="81{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>81,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">81{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> items.
Finally, whether a new task is one where the panel can stand in is decided by two member-level conditions: the distribution of competence and the correlation of errors, both of which we test at the item level (Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B The competence/correlation account in full ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>).
The admissibility test reads both off the same calibration set (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>), so a deployer can estimate before committing whether the panel can stand in.
The frontier judge then needs to be kept only in the dominant-leader regime, for which the test rejects the panel.
To the best of our knowledge, no work in this line gives that price or a measured account of its conditions.
By contrast, we establish both under a single protocol, applied unchanged across eight benchmarks.
Every difference is paired and cluster-bootstrapped, the admissibility test is checked on <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}888" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,888</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}888</annotation></semantics></math> (sub-)panels drawn from the same members, and our harness is calibrated against the published rows it shares (Appendices <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> and <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cascading and routing.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A parallel line reduces the frontier bill without removing the frontier.
Each item goes to a cheap model first, and escalates only when a confidence signal says so.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. [9]</a></cite> report matching a frontier model at a fraction of its cost by cascading, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jung et al. [33]</a></cite> apply the idea to evaluation specifically, and it is now surveyed as a field of its own <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>.
That route optimises, however, a different objective from ours, and the difference is not one of degree.
Indeed, a cascade still issues frontier calls on the items it finds hard, so the evaluated text still leaves the premises, the rate limit still binds, and a retired or silently retrained endpoint still invalidates the pipeline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.
These are the constraints that motivate an on-premises panel in the first place, and no reduction in call volume relieves them.
Within a panel, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. [87]</a></cite> learn from a small labelled audit which judges of a panel to call, on which items, and when to stop, a routing counterpart to our call-every-member stacker, which their own comparison claims to be a strong endpoint wherever its cost is acceptable.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [81]</a></cite> route instead within one judge, between the reasoning and non-reasoning modes of a small open model under a token budget, learning the router from some <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>40,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> labelled preference pairs — what is being routed there is compute, not the choice of judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Cascading and aggregation are moreover complementary rather than rival: a panel with a calibrated abstention would be a natural first stage, which is the direction our confidence-interface limitation points to (Appendix <a href="#A13" title="Appendix M Extended limitations ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">M</span></a>).
We therefore do not position the panel as a cheaper cascade, and where a deployer’s only constraint is cost, a cascade may well be the better instrument.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Closest to our own accounting is <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas et al. [66]</a></cite>, who treat cost as an explicit objective and search judge design decisions multi-objectively against it, likewise favouring open-weight judges for accessibility;
however, they tune the configuration of a <em id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">single</em> judge for pairwise model ranking, whereas we hold a panel fixed and price the substitution it is meant to make, including the labels its aggregator consumes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Purpose-trained judges and specialised detectors.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A competing route trains a single small model expressly for evaluation.
Prometheus does so for rubric-conditioned assessment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, and JudgeLM, PandaLM, and Auto-J for scalable pairwise or single-response scoring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">88</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>.
For grounded factuality, the same route builds compact verifiers:
these include <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">nli</span>- and question-answering-based consistency metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>]</cite>, compact fine-tuned detectors such as HHEM, whose open release was trained on the <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span> training split among other data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>, and LLM-distilled specialist checkers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>.
The last of these are evaluated on the <span id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span> benchmark, from whose test split four of our grounded sets are drawn (§<a href="#S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" title="Benchmarks and judges. ‣ 2. The RAIM protocol ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, such approaches spend their labels on fine-tuning one specialist where ours go to a light second-stage aggregator over frozen off-the-shelf generalists, with no bespoke model to train or serve.
They are the sharpest comparator a cheap panel has, and we treat them as one.
On our class-balanced sets, a published balanced accuracy converts exactly to our primary metric as <math id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=2\,\textsc{bacc}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">bacc</mtext></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=2\,\textsc{bacc}-1</annotation></semantics></math>.
We therefore place those anchors, specialist, guard-tuned, and frontier-prompting alike <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, beside our own panel on one scale in §<a href="#S4" title="4. Standing in for a frontier judge ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (Table <a href="#A6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Harness calibration. ‣ Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).
The guard-tuned row is read off the leaderboard, for the reason Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Purpose-trained cheap judges off their home benchmark ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> gives.
The juxtaposition, however, carries the usual caveats, since factuality-metric comparisons are fragile to exactly these differences of protocol <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.
Nor do we claim that the two are interchangeable.
A specialist is trained for reference-conditioned verification, sometimes on the target corpus’s own training split <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>, and so holds an advantage on its home ground;
yet it cannot score the ungrounded half of our suite at all.
Fine-tuned judges are moreover reported to behave as task-specific classifiers that generalise poorly off their training distribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px9" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.SS0.SSS0.Px9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We close this section with the benchmarks on which all these approaches are compared.
Hallucination resists a single formal definition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, and the eight benchmarks we adopt accordingly span the range, from grounded faithfulness against an explicit reference to ungrounded factuality against world knowledge (§<a href="#S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" title="Benchmarks and judges. ‣ 2. The RAIM protocol ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
State-of-the-art detectors nonetheless remain far from saturating such benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>, which keeps the cheap-panel question open.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A13" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix M </span>Extended limitations</h2>

<div id="A13.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The conclusion names the main limitation, i.e. the roster the panel is built from;
this appendix reports the other conditions we have identified that bound –without overturning– the claims made in the main text.</p>
</div>
<section id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Costing.</h4>

<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our costing is an estimate rather than a quotation.
It prices <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">gpu</span> time at a public reference rate for the card the panel was benchmarked on, and the frontier at list <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">api</span> pricing on one date, so the break-even volume moves with both.
It also prices metered use rather than the hardware footprint a deployer must actually provision (Appendix <a href="#A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2" title="Cost. ‣ Appendix H Open-judge scaling and cost ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>).
We price a label at $<math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, two minutes at $<math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math> per hour;
a domain requiring an expert annotator, of which <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span>’s clinical abstracts are the suite’s clearest case, scales that price and the break-even volume with it.
The outlay nonetheless stays one-time, so it moves where the crossing point falls and not whether there is one.
The costing likewise prices inference and not the orchestration a ten-member panel needs, which a deployer serving the members sequentially pays in latency rather than in hardware (Appendix <a href="#A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2" title="Cost. ‣ Appendix H Open-judge scaling and cost ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Frame sensitivity and quantisation.</h4>

<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The frame is fixed per dataset rather than tuned per judge.
On the four claim-verification sets it is the better of the two frames we ran, for the frontier judge as well as for the panel (Table <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Provenance of the claim-support frame. ‣ Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>).
A frontier-specific prompt search could nonetheless move the <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ExpertQA</span> reversal, which rests on the suite’s weakest frontier score;
few-shot exemplars, in particular, are known to lift frontier fact verifiers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>, and handing the frontier judge our calibration records in that form is a matched-label comparison we do not run.
The open-judge scaling check uses 4-bit <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">awq</span> open judges, so the scaling conclusion is scoped to that quantisation (Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Open-judge scaling and cost ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">External comparisons.</h4>

<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These rest on published data obtained under their authors’ own protocols:
four datasets share their rows with us (Table <a href="#A6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Harness calibration. ‣ Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>), and two more are matched only in metric, on a different slice and, on <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span>, at a different prevalence (Table <a href="#A6.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Harness calibration. ‣ Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>); hence on <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span> we compare levels rather than ranks, and on <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RAGTruth</span> we report only the pattern within the published anchors themselves.</p>
</div>
<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We re-score six published results ourselves.
Two <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-AggreFact</span> leaderboard rows agree to about a point and three <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MedHallu</span> members to within <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.6</annotation></semantics></math> F1, whereas one checkpoint (<span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Bespoke-MiniCheck-7B</span>) we do not reproduce (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Comparability with published results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>).
A cross-paper juxtaposition nonetheless remains weaker evidence than a within-suite contrast <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.
The effective-independence comparison of §<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. The competence/correlation account ‣ 3. Core results ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> is across studies in the same sense:
<math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{eff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>eff</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{eff}}</annotation></semantics></math> are panel-internal and so port between settings, but the tasks, the gold, and the panel size differ, and it is a comparison of a derived statistic and not of a score (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS0.SSS0.Px6" title="Effective independence against a frontier panel. ‣ Appendix B The competence/correlation account in full ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scope of the panel and of its competitors.</h4>

<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We reduce each judge’s task to a binary faithfulness verdict and read each member through that verdict alone;
graded or span-level rubrics, richer aggregators than a stacked logistic regression, and interfaces that expose a member’s confidence rather than its decision are all out of the current scope, and the last of these bounds the panel from a direction we do not measure.
Our competitors are off-the-shelf judges, other aggregators of them, and the purpose-trained detectors, which we run ourselves across the suite (Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Purpose-trained cheap judges off their home benchmark ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>);
we do not, however, re-train a specialist on the labelling budget the stacker consumes.
Although we sweep panel <em id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">size</em> (Figure <a href="#A3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ The rule as a family of thresholds. ‣ Appendix C The admissibility test and its labelling budget ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(a)), we do not vary its <em id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">composition</em>.
We thus characterise when aggregating one fixed roster of frozen generalists helps, not whether another roster, or a matched-budget specialist, would do better.
Symmetrically, the frontier side of the comparison is a single judge, <span id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Claude Sonnet</span>, so the substitution is priced against that model and not against frontier judges at large.
Nor do we measure an escalation cascade, which keeps the frontier judge for the items a cheap model is unsure of.
We read it as complementary to the panel rather than as a competitor (Appendix <a href="#A12" title="Appendix L Extended related work ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">L</span></a>), and leave open what share of frontier calls a panel-first cascade would retain at matched quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Class balance.</h4>

<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every set is built at an exact <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50/50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50/50</annotation></semantics></math> balance (Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Dataset construction ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>), which a deployment stream need not share.
Under a shift in prevalence alone, each member’s per-class recalls held fixed, balanced accuracy is unchanged by construction, whereas <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> is not, depending on prevalence even at fixed recalls, and the identity <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=2\,\textsc{bacc}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">bacc</mtext></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=2\,\textsc{bacc}-1</annotation></semantics></math> no longer holds.
The stacker, fitted on a balanced calibration sample and read at <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, targets to a first approximation the balanced rather than the plain error, so a deployer minimising the latter would shift its intercept by the log-ratio of the deployment priors or, more simply, draw the calibration sample from the deployment stream itself.
We evaluate neither remedy, so our <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> readings hold for balanced evaluation only, and so does the admissibility rule, whose two statistics are computed on the same balanced samples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evidential base.</h4>

<div id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The account is supported at the item level over nearly two thousand points and within every dataset (Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B The competence/correlation account in full ‣ RAIM: Robust Aggregation of Inexpensive Models for Hallucination Detection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>), but the <em id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cross-dataset</em> ordering of the differences rests on eight datasets, so any dataset-level competence/correlation predictor is illustrative rather than confirmatory.
The account and the admissibility rule were moreover formed on these same eight datasets, and with a single clear gain over the best single judge in the suite they are consistent with it rather than validated by it.
Furthermore, the suite never leaves English, its eight sets being drawn from biomedical, encyclopaedic, news, and open-domain question-answering sources, so whether the two statistics keep their reading in other languages or domains is untested.
Finally, both Cohen’s <math id="A13.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> and balanced accuracy inherit whatever label noise the underlying benchmarks carry.</p>
</div>
</section>
